title: Exclusive: Nicolás Maduro and his wife expected to face new charges over alleged torture of Americans
content: Prosecutors in New York are expected to bring new charges against former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores over the alleged torture of Americans who were held in Venezuelan government custody in recent years, according to multiple people familiar with the investigation. An announcement could come as soon as Thursday, the people said. The new charges relate to what the US government has said was the wrongful detention of more than a dozen US citizens in Venezuelan prisons during the time Maduro led a repressive regime in Venezuela, the people briefed on the investigation said. Investigators have also discussed charging several additional people for their alleged role in the torture of Americans, according to a source familiar with the matter. CNN has reached out to lawyers for Maduro and Flores. Maduro and his wife were captured in a US military raid in January from the presidential palace in Caracas. They have pleaded not guilty to narcoterrorism conspiracy and other charges and are held without bail in New York. Flores is expected to appear at a hearing Thursday where her lawyer will ask that she be moved to house arrest ahead of trial. Maduro’s lawyer is challenging the legality of the arrest and argues the former president should have immunity since the alleged conduct occurred while he was in office. The Venezuelan government is not joining in claiming immunity on his behalf, according to the prosecution. More than a dozen Americans were detained by the Maduro government, which was accused by US government and advocates of using them as political pawns. Several of the Americans have spoken out about the torture say they were subjected to while they were imprisoned. Matthew Heath and Osman Khan, who were freed in a prisoner swap in October 2022, alleged in a lawsuit that they were subjected to waterboarding, electrocution, threats of sexual assault, use of mind-altering drugs, and periods of solitary confinement. Heath, a US Marine veteran, attempted suicide while he was detained. The “CITGO 6,” a group of six American oil executives who were lured to Venezuela in 2017 and detained for nearly five years, also say they were subjected to brutal conditions while in Venezuelan detention. In lawsuits filed against their employer — Citgo — Tomeu Vadell, Alirio Jose Zambrano and Jose Luis Zambrano said they were subjected to torture while imprisoned. All of them had been held in the notorious General Directorate of Military Counterintelligence (DGCIM) — which was “responsible for arbitrary detentions, ill-treatment and torture of political opponents and their relatives,” according to a United Nations report. That report found that DGCIM “routinely resorted” to torture practices “including electric shocks, suffocation with plastic bags, waterboarding, beatings, sexual violence, water and food deprivation, stress positions and exposure to extreme temperatures” in order to “extract information and confessions, intimidate, and punish the detainees.” This story was updated with additional information.

title: An Ohio edge. An Iowa tossup. New CNN polls give Democrats hope in a pair of red states
content: Widespread dissatisfaction with the state of the country has opened up a prime Senate pickup opportunity for Democrats in Ohio and made for a razor-thin contest in Iowa , according to new CNN polls conducted by SSRS. President Donald Trump carried both states by double digits in 2024 , and Republicans currently hold both US Senate seats and complete control of the state government in each of them. But in these deep-red states, likely voters now mostly disapprove of Trump’s handling of the presidency, say his policies have increased the cost of living and that tariffs on foreign goods have largely been a negative for their states. About four in 10 in each state say they are financially worse off than they were two years ago. Asked which party they’d like to see in control of the Senate after this year’s midterms, Iowa’s likely voters favor the Republicans (53% to 46%). In Ohio, it’s a more even divide (52% Democrats, 48% Republicans). And in both states, Democrats have the upper hand in the race for governor. In Ohio, Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown holds a 6-point lead among likely voters over Jon Husted, a Republican former lieutenant governor who was appointed to fill the seat vacated by Vice President JD Vance. Brown is more widely known and better liked than Husted, according to the poll, and voters on both sides of the contest say their decision is more about Brown than it is about Husted. Nearly half of likely voters see Brown’s views and policies as about right ideologically, while 43% call him too liberal. Fewer are satisfied with Husted’s positions – 42% call his views and policies about right, 40% say he’s too conservative and 16% not conservative enough. Among Brown’s own supporters, 62% say that choice is more a vote for Brown than against Husted, and likewise, Husted’s voters are more anti-Brown voters (56%) than pro-Husted voters (44%). About 4 in 10 likely voters in Ohio say that which party controls the Senate will be more of a factor in their vote than the candidates’ experience and character or their positions on the issues. Voters motivated by that are split about evenly between Brown and Husted. In order to take control of the Senate, Democrats need to hold their seats in battlegrounds like Michigan, New Hampshire and Georgia while flipping four seats currently held by Republicans. The party’s best pickup opportunity comes in North Carolina, but Ohio may be their next best shot. Iowa, one of several deeply red states at the heart of this year’s Senate playing field , is more of a stretch for Democrats. The poll finds no clear leader in the Senate race in Iowa, with Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson at 45% to Democrat Josh Turek’s 43% among likely voters. Almost 3 in 10 Iowa likely voters say they haven’t yet firmly decided whom to support, and sizable shares don’t yet have an opinion on each candidate. Turek is less well-known than Hinson, with 24% saying they have never heard of him or don’t have an opinion, while 18% say the same about her. Those with an opinion of Hinson break more negative than positive, while views of Turek are about evenly split. In contrast with Ohio, most backers of both candidates in Iowa say their choices are motivated by support for their chosen candidate rather than by opposition to their opponent: 66% of Hinson supporters and 60% of Turek supporters say their choice is in support of their candidate. There are some signs in the poll that Iowa offers a better playing field for Republicans than does Ohio. In addition to likely voters’ preference for a GOP-controlled Senate, Trump’s approval rating here stands at 41% compared with 36% in Ohio and notably above his 34% average nationwide in the CNN Poll of Polls . And in assessing the candidates, more call Turek too liberal (46%) than say that Hinson is too conservative (38%). In both Iowa and Ohio, about half of likely voters call the economy and cost of living their top issue, more than 20 points higher than the second most important issue, the state of US democracy. The economic concerns that have buffeted Trump’s approval ratings nationally all year long are evident here. About three-quarters in each state say that Trump’s policies have increased the cost of living there, majorities say that increased tariffs on foreign goods are a bad thing for their state and roughly seven in 10 say they have faced at least some hardship from rising gas prices. Overall, far more say their own financial situation has worsened in the last two years than say it has gotten better. About four in 10 in each state say they are angry about the way things are going in the country today. Those angry voters express more motivation to vote than do those who are enthusiastic or satisfied with the way things are going in the country in both states. In both states, Democrats lead in the race for governor among likely voters. Democrat Rob Sand leads Republican Zach Lahn in Iowa by 9 points, while in Ohio, Democrat Amy Acton tops Republican Vivek Ramaswamy by 8 points. Both would be Democratic pickups if these margins were to hold. Impressions of Ramaswamy and Lahn appear to be weighing down their candidacies, with the share of likely voters who hold unfavorable opinions of the two Republicans outpacing favorable views by double-digit margins. By comparison, nearly half of Iowa likely voters have a favorable view of Sand – compared to 32% unfavorable – while in Ohio views of Acton are more evenly split. CNN’s Ariel Edwards-Levy, Edward Wu and Isabelle LaBianco contributed to this report.

title: Trump makes third trip to Texas in less than a month despite Ken Paxton audio leaks
content: President Donald Trump made his third trip to Texas in less than a month to stump for a Senate candidate who’s privately questioned his political capital and whom the president has publicly insulted in personal terms. Such is the final sprint to the November 3 midterm elections as the GOP faces an increasingly uphill battle to hold on to the Senate, with the path to the majority running through Texas. Republicans are pouring millions into bolstering state Attorney General Ken Paxton, who polls have shown is facing a closer-than-expected race against Democrat James Talarico in a state Trump carried by more than 13 points in 2024 and that hasn’t elected any Democrats statewide since 1994. Trump’s Wednesday appearance in San Antonio, one Texas GOP strategist said, will be closely watched in the coming days for whether it can improve Paxton’s standing — which could determine continued investment in the state. The president’s latest Texas trip — which comes less than a week after his last stop here — is part of an aggressive midterm travel blitz that has taken him to traditional red strongholds he overwhelmingly won two years ago, including Alabama, Oklahoma and Nebraska. The president has repeatedly told his rally crowds to “pretend” he’s on the ballot this fall, and his advisers believe their best hope for November is boosting base turnout . But some Republicans , even in these red states, are looking for distance from the unpopular president. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott will not be at Trump’s Wednesday evening rally, citing scheduling conflicts. He skipped last week’s Trump appearance too. “It’s pretty clear to me the Paxton team has made the calculation that they believe it’s absolutely worth it,” the Texas GOP strategist said. But as Trump arrived Wednesday, Paxton is also making headlines for seeming to blame the president and some of his agenda for his struggles. The GOP nominee told a group of donors and lobbyists last month that the Iran war and high gas prices are hurting his campaign, according to audio obtained by Axios on Wednesday. “I don’t make the decisions, and I don’t … know what’s behind some of the decisions,” he said, according to Axios. CNN has not independently verified the audio. Paxton’s campaign dismissed the story. “The Attorney General said what every Texan already knows: gas and diesel prices are too high, and hardworking Texans are struggling at the pump and at the grocery store,” spokeswoman Madison Cercy told CNN in a statement, adding that Trump “is doing everything he can to bring prices down.” But that followed The New York Times last week publishing audio of Paxton complaining that Trump’s midterm convention, held last month in Dallas, wasn’t helpful. “So to be honest with you, the numbers — when we did that convention — it dropped our numbers,” the Texas attorney general said. In a statement to CNN, Paxton senior adviser Nick Maddux called the Times story “manipulated nonsense” to “create a story that doesn’t exist.” Paxton has been plagued by his own set of scandals , including securities fraud charges, which ended in a pre-trial agreement; allegations of infidelity; and a 2023 impeachment in the state House (the Senate acquitted him). But that baggage didn’t stop Trump from backing Paxton over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in a primary runoff earlier this year. Their relationship, however, has appeared fraught, even as Trump told reporters in the Oval Office earlier Wednesday that he has no regrets about backing Paxton. At a stop in Denton, Texas, last week, the president called Paxton “one of the most loyal people” — but also “a pain in the ass sometimes.” Then there’s his frequent ribbing of the state attorney general’s appearance. “Some may not like the way he dresses,” Trump said during a speech at the Dallas convention: “I don’t.” Trump did not repeat that refrain Wednesday night, calling Paxton a “fantastic man” as the two showcased warm relations on stage. “I’m very proud of him and I think he’s gonna be an unbelievable senator,” Trump said as he invited Paxton to speak. Paxton, in turn, expressed gratitude to his guest. “Aren’t you guys glad he came to San Antonio?” he asked an enthusiastic crowd. The president “understands how important Texas is to efforts to try to keep the Senate in Republican control, so I think he can put all that aside and probably focus on the bigger picture,” said one Texas GOP operative unaffiliated with the Paxton campaign, granted anonymity to speak freely. “But I’m sure he enjoys making Paxton squirm at the same time,” the operative added. Asked about the candidate’s relationship with Trump earlier Wednesday, Paxton’s campaign pointed to his planned appearance on stage with the president. Paxton’s comments reported by the Times underscore how the president’s unpopularity — his approval rating is 34% in the latest CNN Poll of Polls — may make him an unwelcome guest for some candidates. And he is losing support among a group that helped propel him to victory in 2024. His approval rating among Latino voters was just 27%, according to a NBC News/Telemundo poll earlier this week. Trump may be looking to turn that tide with his visit to San Antonio, where the population is 64.6% Hispanic or Latino. Trump sought to juice turnout among his MAGA base Wednesday evening with a focus on border security and other red meat issues. He attacked Talarico as a vegan — a claim the Democrat has denied. And there were visible efforts to organize, including information about early voting and mail-in ballots for attendees on screens and in handouts. But Trump’s visit, the Texas Republican strategist said, comes with its own risk. “Why go where you can potentially motivate the other side, rather than going to places like Lubbock or Amarillo or East Texas, where you can try to use that brand to actually motivate, you know, the type of voter that needs to turn out for Paxton to win?” the strategist said. There were some signs of discontent. At least a dozen protesters, who interrupted Trump’s rally on several occasions, were removed from the event. And Democrats see Trump’s return to Texas as a good sign for their side. “If you have to pull in Donald Trump four times in the closing stretch of the campaign in Texas, then you have given up on independent voters. This is a loss mitigation strategy,” said one Texas Democratic operative. The Senate race — and the GOP primary and runoff leading up to it — is already on track to be one of the nation’s most expensive. The GOP-aligned bill in Texas is expected to exceed $300 million, with the party and its affiliated groups outspending Democrats by more than 5-to-1, CNN has previously reported . Since the end of the GOP runoff in late May, Republicans have spent $158 million on ads, with an additional $38 million in upcoming ad reservations, according to the ad tracking firm AdImpact. Democrats, meanwhile, have spent about half that: $75 million on ads between late May and Tuesday, with $6 million reserved. But that level of spending in deep-red Texas comes with consequences for the rest of the Senate map. “A lot of us are very disappointed that our predictions have proven correct, and it’s going to cost somewhere between $100 and 200 million to save Ken Paxton as the Senate nominee,” said a Texas GOP strategist who had raised concerns about Paxton during the state’s primary. “If we save Ken and lose the Senate majority because we’ve lost Alaska, Maine, North Carolina, Iowa and Ohio, the Monday morning quarterbacking is going to be biblical,” they added. But Texas has seen close Senate races before, with Democrats’ hopes dashed at the ballot box. Eight years ago, Trump was a key surrogate for Ted Cruz when the senator faced then-rising Democratic star Beto O’Rourke. Cruz, unencumbered by the personal baggage Paxton is carrying this year, won his race by just 2.6 points. That’s led to a debate about how much of this year’s close race is a reflection of the candidate matchup or the national environment and an unpopular president. “If Paxton was a normal person, he probably would still eke it out. I mean, the state’s still structurally conservative,” said one DC-based GOP operative. And the stakes of this year’s race could be bigger than just control of the Senate in 2027; it could carry ramifications for 2028 and beyond. The Texas Republican operative compared a potential Talarico win to a “hole in the dam” that could give Democrats momentum to turn the state blue at the presidential level. Paxton appears to recognize the stakes. “If we lose Texas, we lose America,” he said in a social media post announcing Wednesday’s rally. This story has been updated with additional developments.

title: ‘The list of his failures goes on’: El-Sayed’s Obama criticism resurfaced ahead of campaign rally
content: Former President Barack Obama is set to hit the campaign trail for Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed later this month, years after El-Sayed criticized Obama’s presidency at times as a failure, saying it left the country no “better off.” In comments reviewed by CNN’s KFile from Obama’s 2012 reelection through the 2020 Democratic presidential campaign, El-Sayed faulted him for perpetuating war, eroding civil liberties, overseeing record deportations and preserving economic and healthcare systems that he said favored corporations over ordinary people. He also dismissed the Affordable Care Act as insufficient and argued that Obama’s incremental approach helped create the conditions for Donald Trump’s rise. The comments, made in editorials, interviews and panels, stand in sharp contrast to El-Sayed’s current alliance with Obama, who is now campaigning for the progressive doctor as he faces Republican Mike Rogers in a tight Michigan Senate race that could help determine control of the chamber. El-Sayed’s criticism of Obama was often searing. In a 2012 HuffPost essay written shortly after Obama won reelection, El-Sayed — who said he had voted for him — accused the president of failing to deliver the “hope and change” that defined his 2008 campaign. “This leader has perpetuated war, violated our civil liberties, deported more people from our shores than any other president before him, and the list of his failures goes on,” he wrote. “That memory will serve not as a reminder of the history we made that night – but of the silly emotions of a naïve young man who didn’t understand that hope and change required more than flowery prose and a winning smile,” El-Sayed wrote of Obama’s first election. “I have little hope because there has been less change.” “So let’s be clear, for progressives who care about peace, prosperity, civil liberties, and the future of our country, Obama’s reelection last night was no victory. It was the rock we chose over the hard place,” he added. El-Sayed also took shots at the Affordable Care Act, Obama’s signature accomplishment and legacy across his two terms, calling it a “watered-down reform that kowtows to the interests of healthcare lobbies.” El-Sayed went on to fault Obama across a range of issues, criticizing the expansion of the war on terror into Pakistan and Yemen, the use of drone strikes, the economy, widening inequality and what he described as an erosion of civil liberties. Though El-Sayed made clear he had voted for Obama in both 2008 and 2012, he framed that support as a choice of the lesser of two evils against Republican former Gov. Mitt Romney. In a statement provided to CNN by his campaign, El-Sayed praised the former president. “At 24, I watched President Obama win in 2008. He changed what was possible for someone like me, with a name like mine. Despite being dealt one of the toughest hands of any American president—he handled it. And despite all he did, there remains so much left to do. That’s where the next generation, inspired by him and his leadership, picks up. We stand on the shoulders of giants—and I can’t wait to tell him myself later this month.” El-Sayed’s campaign pushed back on the idea that his past criticism reflected a broader hostility toward Obama, providing numerous examples over the years in which El-Sayed praised him personally. The campaign noted that El-Sayed has repeatedly said Obama’s 2008 victory inspired him to believe someone with his background and name could run for office. It also provided a 2020 exchange in a since-deleted tweet where El-Sayed said he could disagree with “many” of Obama’s decisions and believed the country was “not better off” after his presidency while still viewing Obama as “competent, coherent, and committed to Americans.” His comments were not limited to 2012. Five years later, while running for governor of Michigan, El-Sayed again distanced himself from Obama in a 2017 interview with Vox titled ‘Don’t call this man ‘the next Obama. ‘” Though he praised Obama for expanding perceptions of who could aspire to a career in politics, El-Sayed said there were “a lot of things I disagree with President Obama on” in both domestic and foreign policy and described Obama’s politics as “fairly centrist, middle-of-the-road Democratic policies.” “There’s frustration [among voters] with the fact that they’re being told by elites that their economy is back and that they should just be happy,” El-Sayed said. “But it’s not. Frankly, the economic comeback has largely benefited corporations and has not really benefited people like them.” Still, El-Sayed argued Obama did good things as president, like bailing out the US auto industry, but not enough. “I don’t think he was strong enough on things like health care. I don’t think he was strong enough when it comes to regulating big banks. I don’t think he was strong enough when it came to campaign finance reform, or strong enough on immigration.” A year later, El-Sayed again criticized the Democratic Party in an interview with progressive podcast host Katie Halper in December 2018 after she raised Obama’s response to the Flint water crisis. Asked how Democratic failures helped pave the way for a figure like Donald Trump, El-Sayed said his criticisms came from a responsibility to the people that the government was supposed to serve. “When Democrats buy into an ideology that says that we all ought to focus on the well-being of corporations rather than the well-being of real people, when we forget what suffering looks like, then we make mistakes,” El-Sayed said. He added that voters could then look at the political establishment from both parties and conclude, “you’re all the same, because all of you have failed.” Speaking in January 2020 at a University of Chicago Institute of Politics panel titled “Democrats: Whose Party is it Anyway?,” El-Sayed argued that Democrats needed sweeping structural changes to address inequality rather than more incremental policies, warning that otherwise they would repeat what he called the “same mistakes” of the Obama years. “We are going to continue to make the same mistakes of the past eight years under Barack Obama,” he said. “We are not, as a country, better off eight years after Obama was elected in 2008 than we were when he was elected. And I say this as somebody who loves him deeply.” “Look at where we are right now. Look at where we are right now. We are debating how we beat the most dangerous president in American history,” El-Sayed added. El-Sayed added that while Obama had delivered some important accomplishments, his administration had failed to fundamentally change the economic and health care systems that left many Americans insecure, problems El-Sayed argued helped create the conditions for Trump’s rise. “I appreciate the fact that we don’t give him credit for what he did for the economy in the short term. But the structure of the economy did not change under Barack Obama. The solutions to actually thinking about making sure that our health care system was equitable and sustainable, that did not change under Barack Obama. And unless we’re willing to admit that, then we’re at risk of going right back to the edge of the cliff we fell off in 2016.”

title: Trump’s cheap suit is out of character and awkward for a few reasons
content: The fact that President Donald Trump was photographed flashing a suit tag from a bargain brand of imported suits should not really be news. Any woman in politics would tell you we should not dwell on how a politician dresses. But the fact that Trump, a billionaire, was photographed wearing a suit jacket with tags from Jos. A. Bank, the relatively inexpensive brand, is interesting for a number of reasons. CNN has reached out to the White House for comment. Does the man who bought his own private club at Mar-a-Lago buy suits at the mall? This is the president who sells a $100,000 watch with his name on it and who allegedly inflated his net worth to be included on the Forbes list of billionaires . Status symbols are important to him. He has bedazzled the White House in gold leaf and Corinthian marble and is using taxpayer money, along with donations, to build one of the largest ballrooms on earth. All evidence suggests he likes to appear to be surrounded by the finest things. He accepted the gift of a $400 million luxury jet from Qatar to serve as his Air Force One. But he’s wearing the suit of a sensible sedan driver? The tags on Trump’s suit bear some resemblance to the Traveler collection of suit separates from Jos. A. Bank. The big and tall variant in black is currently on sale for $279 . Advertised as wrinkle- and stain-resistant, it would be a good choice for a trip across the country. Jos. A. Bank is part of a larger conglomerate, Tailored Brands, which also owns Men’s Wearhouse. The larger brand does have some products made in the US, like those from its Joseph Abboud brand, which retail for $700. Jos. A. Bank has an American Bespoke line, which is also advertised as being made in the USA, but the tags featured on the brand’s website differ from those flashed by Trump. That means Trump’s suit was likely made in China or Bangladesh — perhaps not the right message for a president who has promised the return of American manufacturing. The American-made ties by Vineyard Vines advertised on Trump’s online store retail for $125. But that’s just a tie. Just as Trump’s detractors have mocked his very long ties or the overcoat and gloves he wore to greet China’s leader Xi Jinping on a mild Washington afternoon last month, they have also seen reason to pounce on his budget-friendly suit. It’s possible Americans struggling with the affordability crisis might find the choice down-to-earth and relatable, although Trump is hardly struggling. He should be able to afford any suit he wants. His family business has seen investments in cryptocurrency pay off to the tune of more than $1 billion, according to financial disclosures . His company is selling early access to his social media posts, suggesting Wall Street firms who can afford to pay for access will want to use the information to cash in. He is pushing Americans to embrace data centers that could benefit companies in which he is invested. A conspiracy theorist like Trump could wonder if him flashing an inexpensive suit tag might be something done on purpose, to make him appear of the people. That’s been done before — think back to Al Gore’s sweaters or John Kerry’s camouflage hunting jacket or even George H. W. Bush’s cowboy boots. But it’s doubtful this was anything so calculated. Video of Trump opening his suit jacket shows that it occurred during a moment when he was dancing onstage . Taken along with the news earlier this year that Trump apparently bought Florsheim shoes , another relatively inexpensive brand of workwear, for members of his Cabinet, it may simply mean that Trump’s sartorial sensibility is mellowing with age. Trump said the Florsheim shoes were “spiffy” and an improvement over sneakers, a no-no for a Cabinet member. Back in 2016, when he was first running for president, his aide told The New York Times that Trump wore the Italian luxury brand Brioni, “among others.” Trump had previously talked about buying those suits “off the rack.” Brioni had furnished Trump’s suits during his time on The Apprentice. At the time, Trump owned a new luxury hotel in DC and Brioni had a shop there. Trump has since sold the hotel and Brioni has closed the shop. Some others might have wondered if Trump had some incentive to rep the Jos. A. Bank brand. He did, after all, sell swatches from the suit in which he posed for his mug shot in Georgia. He’s sold Bibles , watches , steaks, wine, water — you name it. But the piece of clothing that will always be most associated with Trump is the red MAGA hat, the symbol of his populist following, now for sale at his online store for $55 and made in America . CNN’s Tristen Rouse contributed to this analysis. This headline has been updated.

title: Marco Rubio uses a dramatic backdrop to sketch a post-MAGA foreign policy
content: In the golden light of an Athens evening, with the Acropolis over his shoulder, Marco Rubio hardly looked like a man planning to ride off into a political sunset. The secretary of state’s speech in Greece on Wednesday will surely reignite speculation around his future presidential intentions. It implicitly positioned him as both the heir to and the modernizer of the “America First” movement — just weeks before the 2028 race roars into life after the midterm elections. Rubio depicted the West as a continuous inheritance dating from Ancient Greece to modern America, epitomizing “individuality and relentless ambition, daring exploration and invention” as well as duty and heroism. But he warned that the civilization, ashamed of its achievements and embarrassed by its past, risked “atrophy, servitude and decline.” “Under President Trump, the United States has made its choice. We choose the unapologetic pursuit of national power,” Rubio said, giving himself some political cover for the high-profile appearance. One interpretation is that this was yet another bid to retroactively impose doctrinal coherence on Trump’s erratic foreign policy of Iran war-style gut calls, power grabs and a transactional approach to resources. And Rubio is just the latest administration official to bemoan Europe’s supposed decline; failure to tackle mass immigration; and prioritization of the “global community” over national interest. This canon was hallmarked by Vice President JD Vance’s stemwinder in Munich last year. Yet he was seeking something deeper, at times, sketching the framework of a post-MAGA foreign policy in which US sovereignty and action remain paramount, while​ reinvigorating friendships shattered by Trump’s hostility. “We must rebuild our institutions and alliances” to face new great power rivalries and respond to a “new universe” of threats and attacks, Rubio said. His comments also reinforced a message to decayed European militaries that the US now expects alliances to offer tangible military multipliers to Washington. It was a hint that while nothing will be the same after Trump, a future Republican president might still value updated transatlantic ties. Rubio also seemed to be fusing three strands of traditional GOP foreign policy — the muscular internationalism of Ronald Reagan, the realism of Richard Nixon and Trump’s coercive nationalism. He might also have been trying to make sense of his own political evolution from aspirational conservatism to his current, darker worldview. (Rubio’s critics portray his conversion to MAGAism as the cynical act of a political chameleon desperate for power.) The speech was also jarring and contradictory. He was the latest Trump acolyte to travel to Europe to explain Europe’s history to Europeans and to adopt an idealized view of Western civilization that fits the needs of America’s Christian nationalist right. When Rubio laments eroded national sovereignty, like Vance, he seems oblivious to enduring national and cultural differences distinguishing French, German, Italian, and other European citizens. He ignored gruesome history that led late 20th-century leaders to constrain raging nationalism within shared political and economic structures. And while Trump’s team believes something is rotten in Europe, many Europeans perceive a corrupt and increasingly authoritarian American is most to blame for obliterating Western values. Noting that “passions” have rocked the alliance, Rubio used a deceptive euphemism for Trump’s bullying. Rubio’s lionizing of the ancient Greeks as foundational to the US also overlooked the founders’ concern that their direct democracy encouraged factionalism and promoted demagogues. Their answer was the Electoral College. Some Europeans will be offended by Rubio’s speech. But he’s seen by allies as the most conventional and sympathetic Trump foreign policy official, so his comments may be less provocative than rebukes by Vance or Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Inevitably, such an ambitious speech using the optics of a major campaign address will stir presidential speculation. Visually, Rubio’s setting recalled then-Sen. Barack Obama’s hilltop speech at the Citadel in Amman, Jordan, in 2008. A Rubio run in 2028 seems problematic with Vance in pole position as the vice president. But whether he next takes aim at the White House in two years, in 2032, or later, Rubio showed the world Wednesday his ambition is unquenched.

title: Exclusive: ICE agents told to ramp up daily immigration arrests despite GOP unease as midterms near
content: Immigration and Customs Enforcement leadership told agents nationwide on Tuesday to increase immigration arrests by 1,000 more people daily, returning to a previous goal of 3,000 daily arrests, according to two sources familiar with the verbal directive. It’s the latest sign of ongoing pressure on agents as the Trump administration doubles down on its immigration crackdown despite some Republican unease over who the agency is targeting. ICE also recently released a contract solicitation to expand holding space at agency offices, citing “exceptionally high operational tempo with increased arrests.” With the directive on daily arrests, ICE returns to a previous White House imposed push to arrest 3,000 people a day, an unprecedented number that the agency has previously struggled to meet. ICE had recently been taking around 2,000 people into custody daily on average — a target that officials wanted to sustain. They were also instructed to try to reach 19,000 arrests per week, which accounts for the fact that there are generally fewer arrests over the weekend and not as many officers in the field, one of the sources said. The source stressed that the agency is trying to push officers to arrest as many people as possible for deportation. As a point of comparison, in late June, ICE arrested just over 12,500 people in a week, according to the Deportation Data project , marking a high point. In a statement to CNN, a Homeland Security spokesperson maintained that there are “NO quotas on arrests.” “Under President Trump and Secretary Mullin’s leadership, ICE has been supercharged to find, arrest, and deport illegal aliens from the United States using every lawful tool available. This is promises made promises kept in action, and the results speak for themselves,” the spokesperson said. Immigration remains a key political issue for the White House ahead of the midterm elections, and administration officials have been sensitive to any potential changes in operations that appear to weaken the president’s approach to his mass deportation pledge. That has occasionally fueled tensions between the Department of Homeland Security and the White House. But some Republicans have criticized the administration’s tactics and decision to increasingly arrest undocumented immigrants without criminal records. Florida Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar, who represents a heavily Hispanic district, recently broke with the president in a campaign ad ahead of the midterms. The agriculture industry, which generally leans Republican, also recently raised alarm over an uptick in ICE activity that temporarily disrupted their operations. Immigration arrests had already been increasing. In August, for example, ICE took around 51,000 people into custody, setting a new monthly high for the Trump administration. The previous high had been set just one month prior when the agency arrested more than 46,000 people. Senior Trump officials have repeatedly denied that agents are required to meet arrest quotas, describing the push as a goal, and maintained that agents aren’t punished if they fail to meet that goal. “I have never talked to anybody at the White House about any quota. We do our job every single day and we do it effectively,” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on CNN’s “Inside Politics” last month. “Our focus is to go after the worst of the worst, but when we make contact with an illegal, regardless of how many years you’ve been here, we are obligated by statute to at that point arrest you.” The continued ramp up in immigration arrests has required additional support from contractors. Last month, a contract solicitation reviewed by CNN revealed that the department is seeking contractors to build three different types of temporary facilities meant to help alleviate strain at existing facilities. “Temporary infrastructure is urgently needed to expand secure processing and holding of illegal alien (IA) capacity and non-detained hearing space on site,” the solicitation states. They include a field-detention unit, a room for interviews and processing, and a facility intended to be used for virtual immigration court hearings. A Homeland Security spokesperson said the agency has “no new facility plans to announce at this time.” The agency has also adjusted some of the ways it is conducting operations, including vehicle stops. Last week, ICE officers were told that they’d only be allowed to conduct vehicle stops if they have completed related training courses and must ensure that vehicles used for stops are equipped with lights and sirens, according to internal guidance reviewed by CNN. The memo, which a senior ICE official said amended previous guidance, came on the heels of multiple controversial vehicle stops that have resulted in fatal, and non-fatal, shootings and against the backdrop of internal tension within the Trump administration over how to proceed with the stops, which the administration considers a key tool as it increases immigration arrests. At the time, an ICE spokesperson denied in a statement that the guidance was new, saying: “Occasionally, ICE leadership issues guidance reminders to law enforcement officers.” The spokesperson maintained that vehicle stops will continue and the memo “makes no changes to how ICE conducts vehicle stops.”

title: Takeaways from the first Iowa Senate debate
content: Donald Trump’s shadow looms over every contest in November’s midterm elections — but on an Iowa debate stage Wednesday night, the president’s name was rarely mentioned. The two candidates battling for Iowa’s Senate seat, Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson and Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek, kept their sometimes sharp disagreements on issues like health care funding, the future of Social Security and lowering gas and diesel prices largely focused on the policies at hand — and on branding their opponent as out of step with Iowa voters. The debate highlighted the realities of several Senate races key to the battle for control of the chamber playing out in red states like Iowa. Hinson is seeking to avoid being saddled with Trump’s sagging popularity without alienating a GOP base still loyal to the president. And Turek must win over at least some Trump voters in a state he carried by 13 points in 2024. Turek said he thinks what Iowans want most is lawmakers who will “provide solutions to people’s problems through bipartisan policy.” Hinson, meanwhile, accused Turek of changing his tune and adopting a friendlier posture toward Trump. “You trashed the president during the primary, and now you’re doing ads saying you’re going to work with him. It’s a tale of two Tureks,” she said. Here are takeaways from Iowa’s Senate debate: Turek, vying to reverse Democrats’ slippage in Iowa over the last decade, was clearly focused on attracting independents and moderate Republican voters. For the most part, Turek tried to make the the case that Trump’s policies are “hurting Iowans in a unique way” without mentioning the president’s name. He said tariffs have driven up the prices of fertilizer and other inputs for farmers in the state; that the war with Iran has sent diesel prices soaring; and that the One Big Beautiful Bill Act gutted funding for rural hospitals and left some Iowans who depended on Medicaid or Obamacare subsidies without coverage. He highlighted Hinson’s votes in Congress aligning with the president’s position on those issues, but did so without naming Trump. But in a rarity for a battleground Democrat, Turek also praised parts of Trump’s signature legislation. “When you put together One Big Beautiful Bill, as it’s called, you’re going to have a handful of things that I actually am in favor of,” he said. “I’ve said that, and I’ve been open about it. I agree with President Trump that we need to get private equity out of housing … I believe that we should have no tax on tips, no tax on overtime, no tax on Social Security.” He also bragged that he was willing to buck his own party and work with Republicans in the state legislature. He pledged to “do the ‘full Grassley,’” a reference to the state’s senior senator, Republican Sen. Chuck Grassley, visiting all 99 of Iowa’s counties every year. And he said he would not align with Democrats who might seek to impeach Trump if the party takes control of the House and Senate in November’s midterms. “I have no interest in impeachment,” he said. “I think that we need to look forward, not back. My full intention is to go out there and to work on policy that is going to benefit everyday Iowans.” Hinson, meanwhile, sought to undercut the image Turek aimed to build — while also casting herself as independent-minded and willing to break from Trump. She suggested Turek would “vote like an East Coast liberal.” She also sought to navigate around Turek’s criticism of her votes aligning with Trump on the war with Iran and tariffs — in part by pointing a finger at former President Joe Biden, saying she didn’t want a repeat of Biden’s management of the US military’s withdrawal from Afghanistan or the former Democratic president’s handling of the southern border. Hinson was one of the first Republicans to break with Trump on the war with Iran, calling last month for the president to bring that war to a quick end. And on Wednesday night, she emphasized her willingness to push the president. “I’ll be President Trump’s ally when it is important for Iowa, but I will push back on him — he knows this, because I talk to him regularly — on things that are wrong for our state,” she said. But, she added, nodding to the potential majority leader if Democrats win control of the Senate in November: “Hopefully it’s not Chuck Schumer, but if it’s Chuck Schumer, I’ll work with him.” Both Turek and Hinson said they see a grim future for Social Security without changes to the program. But they had dramatically different answers when asked how they would preserve Social Security’s solvency. Hinson suggested she is open to phasing in an increase in the age – currently 62 – at which retirees become eligible to draw Social Security checks. “If you’re 20 years old, it’s a very different conversation than if you’re at retirement age,” she said. She also said part of the problem is that younger Americans are bad at saving money and suggested “Trump accounts” created by the Treasury Department would help. “Millennials are the worst group of savers in the country right now,” she said. Turek, though, said he opposes changes to the retirement age, and would rather lift the $184,500 wage base cap on Social Security taxes. “I promise you, it’s going to move things significantly in the right direction,” Turek said, adding: “Let’s make sure that billionaires and large corporations are paying their fair share.”

title: British consulate in East Jerusalem will stay open as UK mission, says Ed Miliband
content: Israel and the UK have backed away from a full-scale diplomatic confrontation, with Britain announcing it is rebranding its consulate general ⁠building in ⁠East Jerusalem ​as a UK mission, a move that will result in UK diplomats leaving Israel , with only seven to remain in the building. The move was forced on the UK by the Israeli government as punishment for the decision by the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband , last month to ban trade with illegal settlements and introduce a tougher sanctions regime against those that aided the building of settlements. The UK is seeking to protect the two state solution as the best means of ending the Israeli-Palestine conflict. Miliband has also backed away from a threat to expel a parallel number of Israeli diplomats from London, as was once planned, arguing it would be unwise to do so during the Israeli election campaign. There has been a dispute within the UK government over whether taking tough measures against Israel at such a sensitive political moment could help the re-election chances of the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, before polls on 27 October if they would appear to boost his standing as a leader prepared to confront the nation’s critics. Israel had ​ordered the ‌British consulate ‌in East Jerusalem to shut on Thursday, and the foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, said that it had acted on its threat, describing the consulate as closed. The consulate is separate from the UK embassy, based in Tel Aviv, and has a distinct diplomatic role, covering East Jerusalem, the rest of the West Bank and Gaza, where it provides consular services to Palestinians. Miliband said in a statement: “The UK government reiterates its longstanding view that East Jerusalem is occupied territory.” Sa’ar listed four actions to curtail UK activity in Israel, including the removal of the British representatives from the International Gaza Support Center in Kiryat Gat and entry bans to Israel for 12 named individuals, including the former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn . “We established a clear principle: It is not possible to act against Israel without Israel taking appropriate measures in response,” he said. “We did not want to reach this point, but the actions of the UK Labour government brought us here.” He also accused the UK government of “hostile rhetoric, including false accusations against Israel, such as accusations of ‘ethnic cleansing’”. Miliband, who is currently visiting Kyiv, said in a statement that having ‌withdrawn a number of staff and families in recent ​weeks partly for security reasons, it would be possible to work to build up the presence at the mission in future months. He said Britain would ⁠not take any reciprocal action ​against Israel ​while the ​two sides engaged in ​talks. UK sources said Sa’ar had threatened to close the whole consulate, and it was better for Britain to retain its reduced presence in the hope it could be restored and rebuilt regardless of the imminent election outcome. The sources stressed that the right to take reciprocal action remained, and the UK did not accept that Israel had the legal right to close the consulate, which has stood for 200 years and is placed in East Jerusalem on territory that Britain and international courts recognise as occupied territory. Miliband said the UK mission would be independent, operational and still able to deliver vital services to the Palestinian people. The value of that assertion will be tested by the small number of diplomats remaining and their reduced diplomatic status. The UK national security adviser, Jonathan Powell, travelled to Israel last week to negotiate a version of the deal. It leaves a space, a place and team to build up whatever the outcome of the Israeli election.” Diplomats from other western countries had been worried about any closure setting a precedent, and suggested Britain had to respond strongly to the Israeli move because it had implications beyond the immediate dispute. The ‌incident has highlighted growing frustration among Israel’s longtime allies over its settlements in the occupied West Bank, viewed by much of the world as illegal under international law. In his statement last month to the UK parliament, Miliband said settler terrorists, supported by Netanyahu’s government, were committing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank. Israel disputes this. The UK Foreign Office was advised informally by the former attorney general Dominic Grieve that Israel would be acting unlawfully if it closed the consulate on the basis it was sited in East Jerusalem, which is recognised by the United Nations and most of its members, including the UK, as being occupied Palestinian territory. Israel has also said it will revoke the credentials of Dutch diplomats from the country’s mission to Palestine in response to the Netherlands’ ban on imports from illegal Israeli settlements. France and Canada, which joined the UK in the settlement trade ban, have not had action taken against them. UK-Israeli relations have deteriorated steadily during the war in Gaza, prompted by Hamas’s 7 October 2023 massacre of Israelis, as Britain became increasingly critical of the way in which Netanyahu seemed prepared to tolerate the deaths of thousands of Palestinians in an effort to render Hamas inoperative, a task successive Westminster governments thought was unachievable through his methods. The UK has rescinded a large number of arms export licences to Israel and Miliband has spoken of evidence of war crimes in Gaza. He has declined to accuse Israel of genocide on the grounds he believes this is a matter for international courts to determine.

title: Voting opens in high-stakes Holborn and St Pancras byelection
content: Voting has opened in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection , a contest seen as a key gauge of Andy Burnham’s ability to energise voters and whether Zack Polanski’s Greens can still peel off support from Labour’s left. Polanski, who leads the Greens in England and Wales, is standing for his party in the north London constituency, previously held by Keir Starmer before he stood down as an MP shortly after resigning as prime minister. The seat is, under normal circumstances, a Labour stronghold. Starmer won it with a majority of 11,500 at the 2024 general election despite strong challenges from the Greens and a leftwing independent candidate, who is not standing again and has endorsed Polanski. In 2019, Starmer won by nearly 28,000 votes. Polanski has run a highly energetic campaign . He has mobilised a large numbers of supporters to knock on doors, mimicking February’s Gorton and Denton byelection where the Greens overcame an even bigger Labour majority to take the seat. However, the political landscape has changed. Shortly after Gorton and Denton, YouGov polling put the Greens briefly above Labour, on a peak of 21%. The most recent equivalent had Polanksi’s party on 11%, 16 points behind Labour. Burnham, who succeeded Starmer as prime minister in July, is seen as having revitalised Labour, and used his speech at the party’s annual conference last month to set out a more ambitious and left-leaning collection of policies . Polanski’s fortunes in contrast appear to have declined, especially since last weekend’s Green party conference where a vote by members to adopt a policy equating Zionism with racism and calling for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state prompted condemnation and splits in the party. Four out of the five Green MPs have condemned the policy, while councillors and others have distanced themselves from it or in some cases left the party. While policy is decided by Green members in direct votes, Polanski has been criticised for not saying whether or not he backed the motion and leaving the conference before the vote took place to resume campaigning. The stakes are also high for Burnham. Failure to win the seat by a reasonable margin could end his honeymoon period and bring renewed doubts about Labour’s ability to protect inner-city seats from the Greens, who won several London councils in May’s local elections. Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion Holborn and St Pancras could be promising ground for the Greens, with a young and diverse population that includes many students. About 45% of constituents were born overseas and 48% are aged between 18 and 34. Labour has campaigned hard, fielding as its candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali , the 42-year-old leader of Camden council who arrived in London in the early 90s, speaking no English, after fleeing war in Somalia with her four brothers and her mother, who trained as a lawyer in Somalia. In a pre-poll message to voters, Burnham said: “This area gave Sagal a home when she arrived here as a refugee in the 1990s. Camden gave Sagal and her family hope. Now she wants to give that back to the communities that have always been there for her. It’s hard to think of someone more committed to their local area and the care of people than Sagal.” In his own statement, Polanski said the result was “looking close”, and that voters should choose him to pressure Labour. He said: “We already have a Labour government, a Labour council and a Labour [London] mayor. Isn’t it time for a Green voice for Camden to push Labour to do better on issues like rent controls and to put Thames Water into public ownership – issues where they’ve been backtracking?”

title: All hail the Death Kult of Kemi – captain, coach and owner of the Conservatives
content: W here’s AI slop when you need it? It could all have been so much simpler. Just ask ChatGPT to write me a leader’s speech in the style of Kemi Badenoch . Make it an hour and 10 minutes long, so plenty of room for padding. Go heavy on the slogans, cliches and the obligatory crap politician jokes. Ones we’ve all heard many times before. Not least at this conference. Make the usual digs at Labour and put the boot in to Reform. The main aim of the speech is to try to reposition a party that is tanking in third place on 20% in the polls as the main opposition to the government. And just to give everyone a reason to go home with a feeling of mild optimism, chuck in a retail offer at the end. An uncosted tax cut for people who are rich but don’t feel quite rich enough. The new multimillionaire common-or-garden lower middle classes. Unfortunately, Kemi made the schoolgirl error of trying to write the speech for herself. And it was much the worse for it. What’s the point of having AI if you don’t use it? It was too long, too flabby. No real argument, just a collection of random thoughts. Andy Burnham in Liverpool it wasn’t. Parts of it even seemed to bore Kemi herself. As if she was going through the motions. Lazy, even. That it was still by far and away the best speech of the entire conference is not really the point. More of a reflection of how dire the others have been. Four days of the Tories in Birmingham is a trial for anyone remotely sentient. On the surface, the Tories have seemed a happy tribe this week. There has been a soporific tranquillity to the proceedings. Few members attending, nonexistent queues and above all no Robert Jenrick. Or even Liz Truss. How we miss her. But the unity feels very fragile. The Tories are now Kemi and Kemi is the Tories. The party has bet the bank on her. Kemi even now calls herself the captain, coach and owner of the Tories. Everyone else is an also-ran. This comes at a huge risk. Because Kemi has become almost too big for the Tories to allow her to fail. So they daren’t question her. Anything she does has to be acclaimed as a work of genius. Just walking on stage is enough to secure her a standing ovation. No one has ever quite walked like that before. The party has been captured by the Kult of Kemi. It’s a self-fulfilling prophecy that could lead them to oblivion. They have no idea if Kemi is messiah or lemming, but they are happy to go over the cliff regardless. They are out of other options. Just don’t stop to ask why nothing the Tories seem to do is cutting through. Why the polls are stubbornly flatlining. Why it’s odds-on that beyond the few hundred people in the hall, no one will pay a blind bit of attention to her speech. It will be forgotten within a day. Wednesday morning’s proceedings began with the Tory chair, Kevin Hollinrake. Kev’s dog got a bigger cheer than Kev. Next up was the shadow justice secretary, Nick Timothy, a one-man cluster of antimatter. No man can suck the energy out of the room like Nick. The only thing that would cheer him up is a public execution. Then the Philpster. The UK’s self-proclaimed superhero. The vigilante who took on the French. Endearingly, he still thinks the French navy knows who he is. Chris, most of the UK don’t know who you are. Nor do they care. After this, things began to get surreal as each member of the shadow cabinet was announced and applauded as they took their seats. A bit like a third-rate talent show. The presenter still didn’t know who Nick Timothy was, despite having introduced him moments earlier. She also got Helen Whately’s name wrong. And there was one empty chair. Tom Tugendhat had invented an unmissable trip to India to get out of the embarrassment. Wise choice. A spot of Elgar and then it was Kemi. There was a fight for the soul of the country. There’s always a fight for the soul of the country as far as the Tories are concerned. They don’t seem to realise that it was them that ripped the soul out of it. “What a great conference we’ve had,” she said. It was hard to know if she was being ironic. Other than the fact that everyone has been wandering round in brain-dead surprise that the Tories still exist, it’s been a disaster. Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion After that things went weird. As if we were entering a weird dystopia. Being asked to believe the unbelievable. Like when she said that her shadow cabinet was a united team that listened to one another. This after Kemi had literally said she was the party and that anyone who disagreed with her could go fuck themselves. The whole point of Kemi is that she listens to no one. She also had a pop at Labour for putting all their faith in one man. Pots, kettles. As for Reform, she had nothing but contempt. You’d like to think that would rule out a possible coalition. The one moment when Kemi became truly passionate – believable even – was when she talked about race. This was Kemi at her best, talking about something she really cared about. Even if she did imagine there was no racism in football in the 1970s and 80s. But this bit was all too short and the speech began to feel like it was dragging into eternity. We’d still be trying to stay awake well into the afternoon. Finally the reveal – the inheritance tax reduction that would be funded by as-yet-unspecified welfare cuts. There would be no inheritance tax on anyone leaving their home to their children. With an extra million-quid freebie thrown in, in case you needed to do it up after your parents had let it get tatty. You could hear the cheers from the country’s stately homes echo around the hall. Here was a party that really got it. Which was prepared to do something about the cost of living for the mega-rich. Even as Kemi was speaking, millions of ordinary citizens were phoning their brokers to liquidate their stock market assets so they could upgrade their £1m homes to something far more palatial. The property market in mega-homes had just gone wild. The people’s earl, Charles Spencer, could breathe easy. Althorp was safe. Let them drink champagne. There was just time for Kemi to pay tribute to Jeffrey Archer – the Tories have a soft spot for a convicted conman who ruined several lives – and then came the extended standing ovations. An echo chamber is going to echo. title: ‘People are scared of her, to be honest’: Kemi Badenoch remakes Tories in her image
content: K emi Badenoch has long said that the Conservatives were “under new management”, but in a TV interview to mark the end of a party conference at which she has been front and centre of more or less everything, she took the analogy further. “Your viewers will know that sometimes you have a football team that’s disappointing,” the Tory leader told GB News. “There’s a new captain, there’s a new coach, there’s a new owner, effectively – which is all me.” These are bold words even for a politician known to possess an iron-clad self-confidence. But they are no exaggeration. Badenoch is not only outperforming her party in polling terms, she is busy remaking it in her own image. The broad ideological direction was already set, with Badenoch saying explicitly at the start of this year that centrist ideas were no longer wanted. Some more moderate figures remain in her shadow cabinet, but they are signed up to a right-leaning agenda, including opposition to net zero and a bonfire of human rights protections . Those around Badenoch say, however, that her control goes further, with policy decisions such as the move to grant free childcare to people with incomes above £100,000, announced on the eve of the conference, made simply because she believes they are the right thing to do. “With policies it’s not about chasing certain groups of voters,” one shadow cabinet minister said. “She focuses on what she thinks needs to be fixed, what she feels is wrong.” Talking her out of a policy decision, they said, was a tall order: “It’s not going to happen – it’s tablets of stone. She’s not going to change her mind. She knows what the policies have to be.” Many political parties are, to a greater or less extent, a cult based around the leader, but this is particularly the case for the 2026-period Conservatives, where MPs say Badenoch is talked about on the doorsteps with an admiration and respect not accorded to their party more widely. MPs recount how her name is raised unprompted. One said: “She’s brought up in a positive way. Crucially, in a world where most people couldn’t name more than a handful of politicians, they know who she is.” This starring role was obvious throughout the Conservatives’ conference in Birmingham, not least Badenoch’s arrival, which saw her greeted by a flag-waving crowd of activists chanting: “Kemi, Kemi.” Inside the venue, Badenoch was the heroic centrepiece of the party’s “Birmingham tapestry” , shown in mocked-up 12th-century form doing everything from chastising Wes Streeting to sitting in the turret of a tank. Such veneration is not just wishful thinking by a party eager to move on from a revolving door of previous leaders. While last year’s conference was viewed as make-or-break for Badenoch, even with her party still bumping along at 20% or so in the polls her position is now seen as secure, with the Conservatives more unified than they have been for years. This is in part the result of some serial malcontents leaving for Reform UK, especially Robert Jenrick , as well as the party’s diminished size in the Commons, which as one shadow cabinet minister notes, is too small for factions: “We could just about fill a corner table in Pizza Express.” There are still private doubts, including Badenoch’s instinct to lean into culture wars rather than focus on the economy, which those around her believe is the party’s strongest electoral card. Some party figures also wonder if Badenoch is thinking about election strategy at all with her very personal suite of policy choices, which in Birmingham mainly consisted of giving tax breaks to wealthier people. This was capped in her end-of-conference speech with the announcement that a Badenoch-led government would exempt people’s homes from inheritance tax, an idea which, given that the levy only begins on property worth more than £500,000, is a largely theoretical idea outside London and the south-east of England. While such policies could be appealing to prosperous home counties voters who defected to the Liberal Democrats in 2024, this does not seem to be the plan. During another TV interview, Badenoch chided her questioner for suggesting her tax cuts were aimed at bringing back such support. “I’m very sad that you’re looking at this in crude electoral terms,” she said. “That’s how we’ve all got into this problem where we keep thinking about winning elections rather than thinking about what works.” One former Tory strategist said there was a risk of incoherence: “I can’t understand what is being achieved with these announcements. Forget lots of the small ones, just use the money and do a big tax cut for middle earners.” There was, they added, little chance things would change: “People are scared of her, to be honest. I think a lot of her team don’t know how to say no to her.” However, much like football, politics is not a one-person game, and a star player or manager will only get you so far. And while Badenoch was at pains to praise colleagues in her speech, it is fair to say that the rest of the shadow cabinet is lagging. Andrew Griffith, Badenoch’s new shadow chancellor, was feted by his boss for his private sector business expertise. But on Monday he gave a speech widely seen as one of the worst delivered to any conference in years. It is a matter of profile as well as ability. While Badenoch is recognised by 90% of voters, according to YouGov polling, only 22% say they know who Griffith is. A number of his colleagues are on similar ratings, with pollsters saying even these are likely to be inflated by people who don’t want to admit ignorance. The experienced Tom Tugendhat, now in the foreign affairs brief, does slightly better, on 46%. Laura Trott, the shadow education secretary, hits 50%, but this is because some people mistake her for the Olympic cyclist, now Laura Kenny, formerly of the same name. There was some unease in Birmingham about Badenoch blotting out everyone else. “Isn’t there a danger we are becoming a one-woman party?” one activist asked a fringe of shadow cabinet members. Others disagree. “It’s a normal dynamic for an opposition party that is unpopular,” said Nick Timothy, the shadow justice secretary. “It needs a strong popular leader that can pull it up and we should thank our lucky stars that we have her.” Either way, most Conservatives now accept that, for now, it is up to Badenoch to chart the Conservatives’ course, whatever it involves. One ally said: “We win elections on the economy but there’s no point telling Kemi not to do anything.”

title: Ancient Egyptians sacrificed servants when kings died, forensic tests show
content: Forensic examination of human remains found around the funerary complexes of Ancient Egyptian kings has uncovered evidence that they belonged to servants who were sacrificed when the monarchs died, according to a new study. The remains of these servants, or retainers, were first excavated from the funerary complexes at Abydos, eastern Egypt, which date from around 3000 BC, in the 1920s. Archaeologists at the time suspected that the individuals had been sacrificed, but no evidence of their cause of death was found, study author Roselyn A. Campbell, a postdoctoral researcher at Purdue University in Indiana who examined the skulls from that original excavation, told CNN on Monday. “By consulting modern forensic studies and advances in our understanding of how human bodies react to injuries and to decay processes over time, I was able to identify clear evidence of head injuries in some of these individuals that occurred around the time of death,” she said. “These injuries, combined with the archaeological context, strongly suggest that at least some of the retainers were killed and then buried around the tombs of these rulers,” Campbell added. It was the “sheer number” of graves that led Flinders Petrie, the British archaeologist who originally excavated the remains in the early 20th century, to suspect that the burials were a result of human sacrifice, according to a news release. “In many cultures, retainer sacrifice is practiced because of beliefs that the sacrificed individuals will continue to serve the ruler in some kind of afterlife, but retainer sacrifice can also be a visceral display of the ruler’s power,” Campbell said in the release. “Some retainers might have volunteered to die to achieve eternal life or honor, others may have been chosen or even forced.” Petrie took photographs of the remains and kept records. He then reburied most of them, apart from the skulls, 46 of which Campbell found at Cambridge University. “The injuries on the preserved crania are generally linear fractures, which would likely cause rapid unconsciousness, internal bleeding, and death,” Campbell said in the release, adding that linear fractures are generally caused by a flat, wide weapon. Of the 46 preserved crania examined as part of the study, potentially lethal trauma was found in 18 of them, equivalent to 39%. Campbell cautioned that this doesn’t mean that the hundreds of other burials in these areas were also victims of human sacrifice. “With such a small and incomplete data set, and so many millennia having passed since these people were buried, we simply can’t be entirely certain if all these individuals were sacrificed, or only some of them, or if there is some other explanation that has been lost over time,” she said. Some of them may have died naturally, or others may have been killed by asphyxiation or another method that isn’t visible, she added. Katherine Slinger, a lecturer in Egyptian Archaeology at the University of Manchester, England, who was not involved in the study, told CNN that while it had long been assumed that the royal retainers were sacrificed when a king died, little detail was known about the practice. “The manner in which these retainers were killed has previously remained unclear, with theories ranging from strangulation to poisoning,” Slinger said. “This is the first time that forensic evidence has supported this theory of human sacrifice and proved the manner in which at least some of these individuals were killed.” Campbell is now preparing a book manuscript on the topic, slated for publication in 2027, which will look deeper “into who these retainers were, the context of Egyptian thought and society at this time, and more broadly how we study and understand violence and sacrifice in the past,” she said. Karl Harrison, a forensic archaeologist at the University of Exeter, England, who was not involved in the study, told CNN that the findings are “genuinely really interesting.” However, he warned against over-interpreting the intentions of the ancient Egyptians. “While forensic science can help to understand patterns of injury, care must be taken in assessing what this means in terms of intentionality,” Harrison said via email. “Ephemeral behaviours of past human cultures — especially those without written records or recorded in the writings of other peoples — offer a social complexity that defies our ability to comprehensively reconstruct,” he added . The study was published in the journal Frontiers on Monday.

title: Chinese runner dropped by sponsor after riding bike during marathon
content:
A Chinese fitness influencer has been dropped by her sponsor after she apologised for riding a bicycle during the Berlin marathon.
Sun Yuanyuan, known as Abeeeer on Chinese social media, had claimed a personal best during the event which was held in September.
But an Instagram page dedicated to monitoring inaccurate or misleading race times posted by influencers published a picture which appeared to show Sun on a bicycle between the 35km and and 40km marks.
Sun apologised and admitted to "breaking the rules". Brooks, the running shoe company, has ended its sponsorship deal with her and her finish time has been disqualified by the marathon organisers.
An Instagram account calling itself the Official Marathon Time Integrity Unit (OMTIU) posted a photo of Sun apparently on the back of a bike being ridden by another person during the marathon.
The page also posted a grid of Sun's "splits" - which are the times taken to complete different 5km segments of the race.
The grid appears to show that she sped up between the 35 and 40km marks, when she was allegedly on the bike.
Sun posted an apology on the Chinese social media platform Rednote, which was shared by OMTIU, admitting that she had broken the rules.
She wrote: "I won't make any excuses for this behaviour.
"I was feeling physically unwell on the course, [but] that is absolutely not an excuse for breaking the rules.
"My attempt to take a shortcut was disrespectful to the fairness of the competition and the spirit of the marathon."
Sun, who has 520,000 followers on Rednote, also said she "deliberately concealed" her actions, adding: "I feel deeply guilty about this."
Brooks confirmed to BBC News that it had dropped Sun.
A company statement said: "Brooks believes running should be grounded in integrity, fairness, and respect for competition.
"After verifying the facts, Brooks China terminated its relationship with the individual and publicly addressed the matter."
OMTIU was set up to highlight "the growing trend of GPS-based fabrication, selective Strava displays and false PR claims" among marathon runners, particularly fitness influencers. Strava is a fitness tracking app.
The page's mission statement says: "We exist to protect the integrity of the sport by ensuring that the times athletes share publicly reflect the times they actually ran."
Its Instagram bio describes it as "satire".
BBC News has contacted the Berlin Marathon for comment.
Agata Rutkowska, who has recently suffered health complications, says it is a "big achievement".

title: 'I won Gladiators - now I'd love to become one'
content:
Having been bashed, bumped and bruised on his way to winning Gladiators earlier this year, you might expect Josh McDonald wants to put his feet up.
But the Glasgow fitness coach has not only signed up for another go on the famous Eliminator challenge - he fancies becoming one of the Lycra-clad stars.
The 29-year-old triumphed in the third season of the popular programme , which was filmed in Sheffield last year.
He is now getting the chance to go again on games like Duel, Gauntlet and The Wall as part of a live tour across the country.
Several new Gladiators have joined the show for the new season, including three-time World's Strongest Man champion Tom Stoltman.
And Josh admitted he wouldn't mind "turning to the dark side" and joining the likes of Viper, Legend and Scotland's own Sabre .
He said: "I'd love to be a Gladiator and I think I'd be fantastic at it, with the message I bring, the personality I've got and the athletic ability I have.
"The problem is that while the gladiators are the pinnacle, they can't actually win the show - only the contenders can do that, and I'm really competitive.
"So you're better off being a contender than a Gladiator in some ways, as I don't think you would get the emotional rollercoaster that a contender will get from it.
"But if the opportunity to be a Gladiator came up, then I'd be there."
Josh was actually edged out in the first round of the show, but returned in the next stage after an injury to another contestant .
He did not let his second chance slip away, storming through to the final and taking the trophy after beating Tyler Spence, a teacher from Wigan, in a closely-fought contest.
However while Josh was jubilant to win the competition, the victory also brought with it a mixture of emotions.
He first watched the show growing up alongside his mother Clare, a single parent who raised him and his two younger brothers.
But in 2024, a few months before he got the offer to appear on the programme, his mother died after a long illness.
Josh then became the guardian of his younger brother Max, who was 14 at the time.
"I used to watch the show growing up with my mum," he recalls.
"She loved Wolf [from the 90s version] and it was something you'd sit on the couch going 'oh I could do that, I'd love that' and then the opportunity came up.
"Just before the show [was filmed] I wasn't taking care of myself as much, as I had lost my mum and was taking guardianship of Max and having that extra responsibility.
"There was a motivation of trying to prove myself that I could still compete and give Max something to cheer about, so I got back in training again."
